# Dieulafoy lesion

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Clinical problems > Dieulafoy lesion*

[Original Article Link](/library/d90omR)

---

## Summary

A Dieulafoy lesion is a vascular anomaly characterized by an abnormally large, <u>tortuous</u> <u>submucosal</u> <u>artery</u> that erodes the overlying GI <u>mucosa</u>, leading to severe and sometimes recurrent bleeding without a primary <u>ulcer</u>, inflammation, or other vascular abnormality. It typically manifests in the fifth decade of life and more commonly occurs in men than women. Dieulafoy lesions account for a small percentage of acute GI bleeds, and the exact cause is unknown. The most common location for the lesion is the <u>stomach</u>. Clinical features include <u>melena</u>, <u>hematemesis</u>, and signs of <u>hemodynamic instability</u>. The diagnosis is primarily made via <u>esophagogastroduodenoscopy</u> (<u>EGD</u>), which may need to be repeated. If <u>EGD</u> is inconclusive, <u>CT angiography</u> or conventional <u>angiography</u> may be performed. Management begins with hemodynamic stabilization, followed by first-line <u>endoscopic hemostasis</u> (e.g., <u>band ligation</u>, clips, thermal coagulation). For refractory or recurrent bleeding, options include <u>angiographic embolization</u> or <u>surgery</u>.
